strengths: The paper addresses an practically relevant problem: the safety-helpfulness trade-off in safety fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed two-step routing framework (lightweight prompt-safety classifier + conditional application of a safety LoRA adapter) is a sensible and interpretable design.

The empirical observation that plain LLMs internally recognize unsafe prompts yet still generate unsafe responses is an interesting and potentially useful insight, and the finding that a simple MLP on the last-token hidden state outperforms both Llama-Guard and a sequence-level Transformer classifier is clear and actionable.

The layer-wise probing analysis (Figure 2) showing safety-relevant information is available from roughly the middle layers connects nicely to prior work on layer redundancy and suggests cheaper early-exit detection.
The linear interpolation of LoRA weights (Figure 1) is a clean way to visualize the safety/helpfulness trade-off of the adapter.
weaknesses: The central claim—that the proposed two-step framework improves the safety/helpfulness trade-off—is never evaluated end-to-end. The paper evaluates the safety fine-tune (Section 3) and the detector (Section 4) separately, but never reports results of the combined system (safety score on WJ-Test, quality retention on benign data, latency/overhead of routing).

The evaluation is extremely narrow. Only Mistral-7B is studied, the benign data is limited to MMLU-R multiple-choice questions, which is an unrepresentative proxy for natural benign instructions; false-positive rates are therefore not credibly established. There is no held-out out-of-distribution benign or malicious test set, and no evaluation on adversarial/jailbreak prompts beyond WildJailbreak, despite the paper's own critique of Llama-Guard for poor generalization to new jailbreaks.

No statistical rigor: results are single numbers without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though the paper claims differences are or are not 'significant' (e.g., safety prompt showing 'no significant increase').

Limited novelty: representation-based probing for safety/refusal is well-studied (the paper itself cites Li et al. 2024 on safety layers, plus activation-editing work such as PaCE and SEA), and conditional adapter routing is a known idea. The contribution is largely a replication/confirmation on one model and one dataset, with limited new understanding beyond existing findings on layer redundancy (Gromov et al., 2024).

The training and evaluation details of the proposed classifiers are under-specified: dataset splits, class balance, training hyperparameters, number of training prompts, and how WJ train labels are derived are not reported, and no code release is mentioned, which harms reproducibility.
The Transformer detector's poor MMLU-R accuracy (0.85) is explained as 'overfitting' without evidence; no analysis (e.g., failure cases, confusion by domain) supports this interpretation.

Presentation issues: the main text is very short (roughly 3 pages of content), Figure 2 reports accuracy only on a validation split of the training distribution rather than on a test set, and there is no dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion despite the safety topic; only a brief mention in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper is clearly and concisely written, and the central observation that a plain LLM (Mistral) can recognize unsafe prompts via a simple prompt yet still generates unsafe responses is genuinely interesting and quotable.

The empirical finding that a simple MLP on the last-token hidden state matches or beats a full-sequence Transformer detector, and that safety information is already present from mid-depth layers (Figure 2), is a useful and practical ablation for lightweight safety probing.

The LoRA interpolation analysis (Figure 1) is a clean way to visualize the safety-vs-helpfulness trade-off, and the two-step conditional-adapter framework is a sensible framing for decoupling safety and utility.
Honest reporting that Llama-Guard has high false negatives on jailbroken prompts (0.56 WJ-Test accuracy) adds a practically relevant data point.
weaknesses: The proposed framework is never evaluated end-to-end. The paper claims a two-step routing system (base model for safe prompts, safety LoRA for flagged prompts) but reports no experiment demonstrating this routing in practice, no end-to-end safety score of the full system, and no measurement of generation quality preserved on benign prompts. The central claim 'enhances safety without compromising generation quality' is therefore unsupported.

The baseline comparison in Table 1 is unfair in a way that inflates the contribution: the MLP/Transformer detectors are trained on the WJ training set and evaluated on the WJ test set (in-distribution), while Llama-Guard and prompted Mistral are used zero-shot. Beating a zero-shot guard model with an in-distribution trained probe does not establish superiority.

Generalization claims are not tested despite generalization being a headline motivation. Only one model (Mistral-7B), one safety dataset (WJ), and one benign dataset (MMLU-R) are used. There is no out-of-distribution jailbreak evaluation, no held-out harmful categories, and no adversarial-but-benign data. MMLU-R is a weak proxy for 'benign' — false positive rates on realistic, ambiguous, or adversarial benign prompts are unknown.

The claimed trade-off magnitude is questionable: the MMLU scores in Figure 1 vary only between roughly 0.558 and 0.568, and Mistral's ~0.56 MMLU is far below published values, suggesting an unclear evaluation protocol (few-shot setting, parsing, etc. are not described). The differences may not be meaningful without error bars, which are absent everywhere.

Probing hidden states for safety/refusal is well-trodden territory (the paper itself cites Li et al. 2024 on safety layers; related probing/refusal-direction and routing literature exists), yet the related work discussion is thin and the delta over prior findings (e.g., safety representations concentrated in later layers) is not clearly articulated.

Adversarial robustness is unaddressed: a prompt-level classifier is trivially evadable by adaptive attacks, which is the standard threat model for jailbreaks. A paper whose contribution is a safety classifier should discuss or evaluate this; the limitation is not acknowledged.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release, no training hyperparameters for the LoRA or the probes, no dataset sizes or class balance, and the 'Safety Score' metric (how unsafe responses are judged) is never specified — presumably an LLM judge, but which one is not stated.

The paper is very short even by workshop standards; Sections 3 and 4 read as preliminary experiments rather than a full ICML contribution, and there is no limitations or ethics discussion despite fine-tuning on jailbreak data.

Some inconsistencies undermine confidence: the abstract claims classifiers from 'different model layers perform comparably on the latest model layers' while Figure 2 shows a probe on WJ validation data (in-distribution) with a visible performance spread, and the abstract claims 'minimizing false positives on benign data' based only on a single non-adversarial benchmark.

strengths: The core empirical observations are interesting and clearly stated: (1) safety-adapted LoRA fine-tuning degrades helpfulness (Figure 1's interpolation analysis is a nice, interpretable way to show the trade-off), (2) plain Mistral can *recognize* unsafe prompts under a simple detection prompt yet still generates unsafe responses, and (3) a lightweight MLP on the last-token hidden state achieves a better WJ–Test/MMLU-R balance than Llama-Guard or a 2-layer Transformer detector.

The layered linear-probing analysis (Figure 2) showing safety-relevant information is already present from roughly mid-depth is a useful, consistent finding that connects to the residual-stream literature (Gromov et al., 2024) and suggests practical efficiency gains (probing at intermediate layers).

The paper is well written and easy to follow, with honest framing of limitations in the conclusion (oversensitivity, generalization concerns), and the appendix provides enough architectural and prompt detail to begin reproducing the detectors.

The conditional-routing framing (lightweight detector + safety adapter applied only when needed) is a sensible, practical alternative to unconditional safety fine-tuning and avoids the false-positive costs discussed in the introduction.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow: a single base model (Mistral-7B), a single safety fine-tuning dataset (WildJailbreak), and essentially one benign test set (MMLU-R) used as a proxy for false positives. Claims that 'LLMs encode safety information' or that the framework generalizes cannot be supported from one model/dataset pair; no other base models, LoRA configurations, or out-of-distribution jailbreak families are tested.

The proposed two-step framework is never evaluated end-to-end. The paper motivates conditional adapter routing but reports no results for the assembled system (benign generation quality, unsafe-prompt refusal rate, latency overhead of running the detector). The actual contribution risks being 'probing experiments on WJ' rather than the framework in the title/abstract.

Safety-critical claims lack adversarial robustness analysis. A last-token-representation MLP classifier is exactly the kind of component that adaptive attackers can evade (e.g., jailbreak suffixes or prompt perturbations that shift the [/INST] representation). For a paper whose central deliverable is a safety gate, the absence of even a Bearer [REDACTED] evaluation is a significant soundness gap.

The 'Balanced Score' (harmonic mean of accuracy on MMLU-R and WJ–Test) is an ad-hoc metric conflating two different distributions; no precision/recall, no false-positive-rate operating-point analysis, and no statistical significance or variance across seeds are reported for Table 1, so differences like 0.87 vs. 0.88 WJ accuracy are uninterpretable.

Missing related work and baselines from the probing/representation-safety literature (e.g., representation engineering, refusal-direction analyses, safety-neuron work beyond the single Li et al. citation, and textual classifiers such as fine-tuned small models). The claim that representation-based detection is novel is overstated; probing classifiers for harmfulness/refusal on hidden states is a known technique.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or model release is mentioned, detector training details (learning rate, epochs, training set sizes, class balance, number of seeds) are absent, and WJ training details for the LoRA adapter are unspecified.

Several notable findings are underdeveloped: the observation that safety-prompted representations do not improve detector training and that the Transformer detector overfits WJ are presented in a single sentence each, without analysis of why or when this holds.

Scalability of conclusions from a 7B model: whether the mid-layer probing result holds for larger/more-aligned models (where safety is known to be concentrated in specific layers, cf. Li et al. 2024) is left open but not flagged as a limitation of the layer-wise claim.

strengths: The paper is technically sound overall. The core method (Gaussian Discriminant Analysis / Mahalanobis-distance classification over last-token hidden states) is simple, clearly specified (shared covariance, ridge-regularized precision estimate, FFN output of the final block), and the supporting analyses are unusually thorough for this kind of paper: layer-depth ablation (Fig. 6a), few-shot sample-size ablation (Fig. 6b), shared vs. per-class covariance ablation (Appendix E), min/avg/max across ten prompts (Fig. 3, Tables 7-8), and a per-category error analysis with discussion of annotator ambiguity (Appendix C, Table 6).

Evaluation breadth is a major strength: 8 harmful and 7 neutral benchmarks, three base model families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo) spanning 1B-32B plus a MoE variant, and comparison to three established guard models (Aegis, LlamaGuard 1-3, WildGuard) on a matched-parameter footing.

The empirical observation in Section 3.1/3.2 (models recognize harmful prompts when asked but still comply when not asked; prompted base models can rival guards) is interesting and well supported by Figure 2 and the prompt-sensitivity tables, and gives the paper a genuine insight beyond the method itself.

The hierarchical-prototype mechanism provides a credible answer to the 'emerging risk' adaptability criticism of guard models (Fig. 4a/b), and Section 5.4 on pretrained vs. instruction-tuned base models is a useful empirical contribution in its own right.
Limitations and impact are addressed honestly: the paper acknowledges dependence on the base model's representations and restricts scope to input moderation.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the paper's own evidence: the abstract and Section 5.1 state that OLMo-based LPM 'achieves the best overall results and beats all the guards', yet Table 1 shows LPM-M(OLMo2-7B) at 89.44 average F1 versus WildGuard's 89.93, i.e., LPM does not surpass the strongest guard on the headline harmful-prompt metric (it wins only on neutral TNR). The text should be corrected to 'matches'.

Novelty is modest. The core classifier is standard Mahalanobis/GDA classification of hidden states, well established in OOD detection (which the paper itself cites via [29]); the contribution is largely an application and careful evaluation of known distance-based classification to prompt safety. Reviewers building on representation-based safety work may see this as incremental.

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading. LPM requires a labeled set of safe and harmful prompts (tens of thousands per class in Fig. 6b) to compute prototypes/covariances, plus forward passes over that data; this is few-shot calibration, not training-free in the sense practitioners might assume. The distinction deserves sharper treatment, including the fact that prototype data can come from datasets closely related to evaluation data (e.g., WildGuardMix vs. WildJailbreak), which may inflate results relative to guards trained on different mixtures.

Reproducibility is weak: the only reproducibility statement is the GPU type. No code or prototype-set release is mentioned, and important details (exact prototype dataset composition, regularization strength for the ridge estimator, prompt template used for LPM tokenization) are not pinned down in the main text.

Some results reveal instability that is under-discussed: the Euclidean variant shows extreme failures (e.g., 54.78 TNR on Alpaca and 0.00 F1 on GSM8k-related neutrality for Mistral-7B in Tables 3-4), and Figure 6b shows large variance in low-sample regimes; the practical implications for real deployments (threshold-free nearest-prototype may silently degrade on new model families) deserve more caution than the currently confident framing.

Guard-model comparison fairness could be questioned: guards handle multi-label taxonomies and input+output moderation, while LPM is binary input-only; the paper does not discuss the operational cost of maintaining/labeling prototype sets versus fine-tuning an existing guard on new categories.

strengths: The core observation is interesting and well-motivated: instruction-tuned LLMs can often verbally recognize unsafe prompts they would still answer harmfully, and safe/harmful prompts appear separable in latent space. This 'gap between internal representations and surface behavior' is a genuinely useful insight for the moderation literature.

The evaluation breadth is commendable: 8 harmful datasets spanning vanilla and adversarial prompts, 7 neutral datasets for true negative rate, and three model families plus size/MoE variants (Figures 1b, 5, 6, Appendix B). This is more comprehensive than typical guard-model papers.

The paper includes a thoughtful set of ablations: layer choice (Fig. 6a), number of samples per class (Fig. 6b), shared vs. per-class covariance (Appendix E), hierarchical prototypes for emerging risk categories (Fig. 4), and an error analysis with concrete examples of ambiguous labels (Appendix C).

LPM is practical: negligible inference overhead, works on small (1B) models, and the hierarchical-prototype mechanism offers a credible story for adapting to new risk categories without retraining, which guard models cannot easily do.
Appendix D transparently documents prompt variance for the prompting baseline, which honestly motivates the move away from prompt-based assessment.
weaknesses: The headline claim is overstated. Table 1 shows WildGuard achieves 89.93 average F1 while the best LPM variant (LPM-M(OLMo-7B)) achieves 89.44, yet the paper claims LPM 'even surpasses our strongest guard baseline, WildGuard' (Sec. 5.1) and 'matches or exceeds state-of-the-art guard models' (Abstract). This is only true relative to some guards and in cherry-picked configurations (e.g., the MoE point in Fig. 1b), not against the strongest baseline in the main comparison.

A critical baseline is missing: a linear probe (e.g., logistic regression) trained on the same hidden states and the same labeled safe/harmful data. LPM is essentially Gaussian Discriminant Analysis on last-token hidden states, and the field's standard cheap baseline for 'safety information in representations' is a trained linear classifier. Without it, the claim that Mahalanobis/prototype classification is the right tool—and that anything 'special' about latent safety structure is being exploited—is unsupported. Related probing/representation-engineering literature (e.g., [31,37,48,50], latent-space safety direction work) is cited but not empirically compared.

The 'training-free' framing is misleading. LPM requires a labeled dataset of safe and harmful prompts, computes class means and a (ridge-regularized) precision matrix from them, and performs supervised classification at inference. This is supervised classifier fitting without gradient descent; the practical distinction from a lightweight trained probe or LoRA-tuned guard is not clearly established, and the claimed cost advantage over 'training guard models' is blurred.

Considerable fragility is visible in the appendix but not confronted in the main text. Table 3 shows LPM-E variants with catastrophic true negative rates on neutral data (e.g., LPM-E(Mistral-7B) 47.29, LPM-E(Llama-8B) 72.72, several near-random on BBH/Codex/MTBench), and Table 4 shows XSTest F1 as low as 1-2 for some variants. The main table presents only the favorable instruction-tuned configurations, so the method's robustness across model versions is substantially weaker than the narrative suggests.

Evidence for the central latent-space separability claim rests on a t-SNE plot (Fig. 1a), which is well known to be visually persuasive but quantitatively uninformative; no quantitative separability metric or comparison across layers/choices is provided there.

Evaluation methodology concerns: F1 scores are averaged across datasets with wildly different sizes and class balances (Table 2) without weighting or significance testing; guard models are compared on F1 alone even though operating points (precision/recall trade-offs, thresholds) differ; no variance or confidence intervals are reported for LPM results, while Figure 3 shows large prompt-driven variance for the prompting baseline.

Reproducibility provisions are minimal: the statement lists GPU hardware only, with no mention of code or prototype/covariance release. Given the method's simplicity, releasing exact extraction details (which token, which FFN output, prompt template used at extraction) is essential, but Appendix D covers only the prompting baseline prompts, not LPM extraction specifics.

Presentation issues: Figure 1b lacks axis clarity for comparing guards vs. LPM fairly (model size on x-axis conflates family and training data differences, which footnote 2 itself acknowledges); Figure 3 is dense and hard to read; the paper sometimes asserts conclusions ('LPM consistently outperforms LlamaGuard and Aegis on average across all three base models') that hold only for the selected instruction-tuned variants.

strengths: The core idea is simple, practical, and well-motivated: demonstrating that instruction-tuned LLMs internally encode input safety (Section 3, Figures 2 and 3) even when their surface behavior is unsafe is an interesting and useful empirical observation, and LPM turns it into a nearly free add-on for moderation.

The evaluation is broad: 8 harmful datasets and 7 neutral datasets, three model families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo) spanning sizes from 1B to 70B including a MoE variant, with true negative rates on neutral data reported to check that moderation does not break benign usage (Table 1, Table 3).

Useful ablations: layer choice (Figure 6a shows safety features emerge early and results are robust to depth), number of prototype samples (Figure 6b shows good performance in low-resource settings), shared vs. per-class covariance (Appendix E), and a qualitative error analysis by harm category (Appendix C) that honestly identifies subjective categories where LPM struggles.

The hierarchical prototype extension (Section 5.3, Figure 4) directly addresses the 'evolving risks' motivation and shows 2-4% gains from adding prototypes across datasets/categories, supporting the adaptability claim.
Reproducibility support is reasonable: all prompts are provided in Appendix D, dataset statistics in Table 2, and hardware is specified; the method itself is simple enough to reimplement easily.
weaknesses: Missing the most natural baseline: a linear probe (logistic regression or linear classifier) trained on the exact same hidden states. The paper's framing is that latent space already separates safe/unsafe; a linear probe is nearly as lightweight as LPM and prior work has shown safety is linearly decodable from LLM representations. Without this comparison it is unclear whether Mahalanobis prototype classification is actually the right tool or simply underperforms a trivial alternative.

Potential train/test overlap: prototypes (and covariance) are computed from WildGuardMix training data (Figure 1a) and LPM is then evaluated on WildGuardMix test (Table 1), its best-performing dataset. The paper does not clearly report which datasets are used for prototype construction for the main Table 1 results, so the claimed state-of-the-art average (driven largely by WGMix and XSTest) is difficult to interpret in terms of generalization.

The 'training-free' claim is somewhat overstated: LPM requires labeled safe and harmful examples to compute prototypes and an empirical precision matrix (a ridge-regularized covariance inverse), which is effectively fitting a Gaussian classifier. The distinction from lightweight trained moderators should be argued more carefully, especially since the low-data regime (Figure 6b) implies sensitivity to the choice of calibration examples.

Robustness to adaptive adversaries is not evaluated. Since the entire defense is a distance threshold in a fixed latent space, an obvious attack is crafting prompts whose last-token representation lands near the safe prototype. Guard models are routinely evaluated against jailbreak attacks; LPM's behavior under such pressure is unknown, which weakens the 'practical solution for scalable moderation' claim.

Novelty is modest: prototype/Mahalanobis-distance classification is decades old (Mensink et al. [34], GDA), and its application to LLM hidden states is closely related to existing OOD detection and representation-engineering work that the paper cites but does not empirically compare against. The contribution is primarily a careful empirical demonstration rather than a new method or new understanding of why the separation exists.

The headline claim that LPM 'beats all the guards' rests on one configuration (OLMo-2-7B, 89.44 vs. WildGuard 89.93 is actually a loss; only LPM-M(OLMo2-7B) leads). Per-dataset variance is large (e.g., ToxicChat F1 of 45-75 for LPM variants), and several guard models win many individual datasets, so the summary framing in the abstract and Figure 1b is stronger than the evidence.
